title: CS onboarding feedback loop — activation blockers + ideas for emails/nudges
summary: Aparna shared aggregated onboarding feedback from Support + CS + a few recent sales/SE notes. Top activation blockers cluster around: (1) auth and API key confusion (wrong project/org, permissions, mixing keys), (2) first request errors that aren’t self-explanatory (401/403/404, model_not_found, rate_limit), (3) streaming-specific friction (SSE/WebSocket expectations, proxies, SDK version mismatch), and (4) “what model should I pick” / “how do I control cost” uncertainty. Team aligned on what the lifecycle sprint nudges and emails should address: fast path to a known-good curl/SDK snippet, error-driven troubleshooting, a clear activation checklist in-console, and lightweight reassurance on credits/billing and where cost/latency dashboards live. Guardrail callouts: do not over-promise benchmarks, keep support escalation links prominent, and ensure email links land on the right console route (avoid 404s).
topics: First request failure modes (401/403/404, model selection, rate limits)
What to include in onboarding emails vs in-console nudges
action_items: Aparna Reddy — send Ben/Marissa the top 10 verbatim user quotes + ticket links that map to blockers — due 2025-01-24
Dev Patel — draft a short “first request failure triage” checklist for Support and a public-facing snippet version for emails — due 2025-01-27
Marissa Cole — ensure console checklist includes a direct link to API key creation + a ‘copy curl’ test request — due 2025-01-28
Henry Cho — confirm activation definition includes a ‘first 2xx completion’ event and capture common error_code property for failures — due 2025-01-24
Paula Mendes — add instrumentation note: capture sdk_name/sdk_version + streaming_enabled and surface to dashboards — due 2025-01-29
Ben Carter — update email v1: add troubleshooting block + “what to do if you see 401/403” with doc links and support CTA — due 2025-01-27
next_steps: Map each blocker category to a specific email module and a specific console nudge (one-to-one where possible).
Validate that all email CTAs route to current console paths (no deprecated URLs).
Add at least one ‘streaming success’ path in docs/snippets but keep activation primary metric as first successful non-streaming request (lower friction).
Re-review claims in retargeting/email copy to avoid benchmark overstatement; link to canonical benchmark page when used.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: CS onboarding feedback loop — activation blockers + ideas for emails/nudges
Date: Thu, Jan 23, 2025
Time: 9:05 AM - 9:43 AM PT
Duration: 38 minutes

Attendees:
- Aparna Reddy (Redwood, Customer Success)
- Ben Carter (Redwood, Growth)
- Marissa Cole (Redwood, Product - Console)
- Henry Cho (Redwood, PM - Activation milestone)
- Paula Mendes (Redwood, Telemetry)
- Dev Patel (Redwood, Support)


Summary (auto-generated by Fireflies):
- Reviewed top onboarding friction points from CS and Support tickets
- Discussed recommended email and console nudge interventions
- Agreed on priorities: API key clarity, first request troubleshooting, streaming guidance, model selection hints

Topics (auto-generated):
1. API key + permissions confusion
2. First request errors and troubleshooting
3. Streaming disconnects / SDK mismatch
4. Model choice + cost anxiety
5. What to bake into nudges vs emails


[00:00] Aparna Reddy: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone. I wanted to do a quick loop back from CS and Support on what we’re seeing with brand new self-serve folks. This is basically the “why aren’t they getting to first success” stuff, and what we can address with the lifecycle emails and the in-console checklist.

[00:18] Ben Carter: Yep. This is perfect timing. We’re finalizing the v1 sequence and the nudge copy this week.

[00:23] Aparna Reddy: Great. So, I bucketed it. Number one, by far, is auth confusion. Not like, “how does OAuth work,” more like, they created an API key but then they’re using it in the wrong place. They’ll have multiple projects, multiple orgs, and they paste the key into a template that’s pointing at a different project.

[00:44] Dev Patel: Yeah. Or they’re rotating keys and then the old one still sits in their env vars. We get a bunch of “401 unauthorized” and they swear the key is new.

[00:53] Aparna Reddy: Exactly. And our error messages are… okay, but not always actionable. Like “invalid API key” doesn’t tell you “you’re calling the wrong base URL” or “your key is scoped to Project A.”

[01:06] Marissa Cole: Do you see them in Console before they do the call? Or are they mostly coming from docs / quickstart copy-paste?

[01:12] Aparna Reddy: Both. The pattern is: signup → they click around, maybe create key, then they go straight to code. If it fails, they often don’t come back to Console to debug. They instead reply to the welcome email or open a Support ticket.

[01:28] Ben Carter: That’s helpful. So email needs a “if you get a 401/403 here’s the top 3 things to check” and a link into the exact console page.

[01:36] Aparna Reddy: Yes. But link correctness is critical. We have some tickets around 404 because the console routing changed.

[01:43] Dev Patel: Yup, we had at least two last week. Someone clicked “Manage API Keys” and ended up in a dead route, then they assume we’re broken.

[01:52] Marissa Cole: Okay, I’ll take that. We should use a stable route and if we’re using deep links, make sure they redirect.

[01:58] Henry Cho: From a measurement standpoint, we should also track “clicked email CTA to console api-keys page” versus “api_key_created.” But I know that’s the attribution stitch topic.

[02:10] Paula Mendes: Yep, as long as we get the UTM in the event properties. For console events, we can attach last_touch_utm_* if it’s in the browser storage. Just flagging.

[02:20] Ben Carter: Great. Keep going on the buckets.

[02:23] Aparna Reddy: Bucket two: first request errors that look like product bugs but are user setup. Like 403 for permissions. Or “model_not_found” because they use a model string from an old blog post, or from another provider’s naming.

[02:38] Ben Carter: Like they type “gpt-4o-mini” into Redwood?

[02:41] Aparna Reddy: Exactly. Or “claude-sonnet.” They’re coming from OpenAI or Anthropic, and they assume the name is portable. They don’t look at the model catalog.

[02:52] Marissa Cole: We have that model picker in Console, but in the API docs we still show a couple model IDs that are… not wrong, but not the easiest starting point.

[03:02] Dev Patel: Also embeddings folks. They try chat endpoint with an embeddings model, or vice versa. Then they see a 400 and just bounce.

[03:10] Aparna Reddy: Yeah. So suggestion: nudge that’s contextual. If they created a key but we never see a successful request in 30 minutes, show a banner like “Try the copy-paste curl request” with a model that’s known good. And the email can do the same.

[03:25] Henry Cho: For activation definition, this is why I’m leaning “first 2xx completion” as primary, not “first streaming success.” Streaming is a nice milestone but too many variables.

[03:35] Ben Carter: Agree. We can include streaming as a “next step” email.

[03:40] Aparna Reddy: Third bucket: streaming confusion. Folks think it’s WebSockets, but it’s SSE. Or they’re behind a corporate proxy and the stream just hangs. Then they think our service is down.

[03:53] Dev Patel: The tickets read like “it never returns” and then you find out they’re in Postman with streaming not supported the way they configured. Or their Node fetch version is weird.

[04:03] Marissa Cole: Are they mostly Node/TS or Python?

[04:06] Aparna Reddy: Mostly TS/Node for the streaming issues, but Python too. Also some people paste curl without the right flags, so they don’t see incremental output and think streaming isn’t working.

[04:18] Ben Carter: So in the checklist we should have “Make a first request (non-streaming)” then “Enable streaming (optional)” with an explanation. Not required for activation.

[04:28] Aparna Reddy: Yep, and give them the exact known-good snippet. “If you are behind a proxy, here’s what to try.” Even a simple troubleshooting link.

[04:37] Paula Mendes: If we can capture streaming=true/false and maybe the client type, we can quantify how many are attempting streaming before first success.

[04:45] Henry Cho: +1. Also, can we capture an error_code property for failed requests? Even if it’s not perfect, it’ll tell us what we’re optimizing.

[04:55] Marissa Cole: We can do that for the Console-triggered requests. For API calls from customer code, depends if we’re instrumenting server-side. But we do have response codes and some internal error categories.

[05:05] Aparna Reddy: Fourth bucket is like… “what should I do next” and cost anxiety. People get to the console, see a bunch of knobs—routes, deployments, dedicated, private—and they freeze.

[05:18] Ben Carter: That’s the classic “choice overload.”

[05:20] Aparna Reddy: Yeah. They ask: “Do I need dedicated? Is hosted safe? Where is data stored? Do you train on my prompts?” Like day one questions.

[05:31] Dev Patel: Support sees “do you retain logs” a lot. They’re trying to decide if they can even test with real-ish data.

[05:38] Marissa Cole: We should be careful with how we answer in marketing emails. We can link to the security page and say “we don’t train on customer data” but we need the exact approved language.

[05:47] Ben Carter: We have Soojin reviewing. But yes, we can’t over-promise.

[05:52] Aparna Reddy: And a lot of them just want to see cost/latency quickly. They’ll ask “how much does this cost per 1M tokens” before they’ve done anything. So one nudge could be “After your first request, check the latency + cost dashboard” with a screenshot.

[06:09] Paula Mendes: That one helps because we want them to view the dashboard as an early retention driver. It’s a “value moment.”

[06:16] Henry Cho: Right, we can treat dashboard_viewed as a secondary milestone in week 1.

[06:21] Ben Carter: Aparna, do you have concrete examples from CS calls? Like the exact words.

[06:26] Aparna Reddy: Yeah. I’ll send a doc. But one quote is literally: “I created an API key, your docs say set REDWOOD_API_KEY, I did that, but I still get unauthorized. Is this because I’m on the free tier?” That’s a very common assumption.

[06:44] Dev Patel: They think it’s paywalled. It’s not. It’s just wrong key or wrong header.

[06:48] Marissa Cole: Our error message could explicitly say “This is not a billing issue” when it’s a 401, if we can detect that.

[06:55] Henry Cho: That would reduce tickets.

[06:57] Ben Carter: Also in the email: “Free credits are enabled by default; 401 usually means key or header.”

[07:05] Aparna Reddy: Yep. Another one: “I’m calling /v1/chat/completions and it says model not found.” Then you see they typed a model string from Together or OpenAI. If we can make the quickstart pick a default model ID that’s in our catalog and stable, that solves a lot.

[07:24] Marissa Cole: We can do a “Recommended starter model” in the catalog and reference that everywhere.

[07:29] Paula Mendes: Just make sure it doesn’t change under them without notice, or we’ll have attribution issues.

[07:33] Aparna Reddy: Another bucket is “where do I paste this.” People copy an API key but don’t know the header. Or they put it in the JSON body.

[07:42] Dev Patel: That’s… astonishingly common.

[07:44] Ben Carter: We can include a very literal snippet in email 2: “export REDWOOD_API_KEY=…” and “curl -H ‘Authorization: Bearer …’”

[07:52] Aparna Reddy: Yes. The more it’s copy-paste and hard to mess up, the better.

[08:00] Marissa Cole: For Console nudges, one idea is a checklist step: “Send a test request.” We can provide a ‘Try it’ button inside Console that uses their key and makes a request. If it fails, we can show a tailored error state.

[08:15] Henry Cho: That also gives us consistent telemetry for the first attempt.

[08:18] Paula Mendes: And we can capture the error_code property in a normalized way.

[08:22] Ben Carter: But is that in scope for v1? Or is v1 just banners and checklist links.

[08:28] Marissa Cole: v1 is checklist + two banners, per the spec. The “Try it” could be follow-on. But we can do a link to a pre-filled curl with their key masked. Or at least a “copy curl” in the checklist.

[08:43] Aparna Reddy: That’s fine. Even linking to a “Hello inference” page in docs helps. The key is: if they’re stuck, we should not just say “read the docs.” We should say “do these 3 checks.”

[08:56] Dev Patel: Exactly. Like: 1) confirm you’re using the key from the right project, 2) confirm header format, 3) confirm base URL is api.redwood… not the console domain. People hit console URL.

[09:10] Ben Carter: They call the console domain? Wow.

[09:12] Dev Patel: Yeah, they do.

[09:14] Aparna Reddy: They do. It’s not frequent, but it’s enough that it’s a top-10 issue.

[09:19] Henry Cho: We should add an explicit note in the quickstart: “Requests go to api.redwoodinference.com.”

[09:25] Ben Carter: Okay. Let’s translate to lifecycle interventions. I’m hearing:
- Email 1 welcome: set expectations + link to API key creation + the fastest possible “hello world.”
- Email 2 first success: copy/paste curl + common errors.
- Email 3 streaming: optional but with known-good snippet.
- Email 4 observability: show cost/latency dashboard.
- Email 5 next steps: routing / deployments / invite teammates.

[09:52] Aparna Reddy: That’s basically it.

[09:54] Marissa Cole: For nudges: checklist steps should mirror that sequence. And if we can trigger banner based on missing event—like no first_success within X hours—then show the “Try the curl” banner.

[10:07] Paula Mendes: We need to be careful with timing windows and avoid spamming. Also guardrails: if error volume spikes, we should pull back.

[10:15] Dev Patel: +1. Also please include a “Contact Support” link that goes to the right form, not a generic email. When folks reply to no-reply addresses it’s messy.

[10:25] Ben Carter: Totally. We can route them to support portal with pre-filled context.

[10:29] Aparna Reddy: Another subtle one: people are unclear about “projects” versus “deployments/routes.” They think they have to create a deployment before calling hosted.

[10:40] Marissa Cole: Yeah, we’ve seen that. They click into “Routes” and think it’s required.

[10:45] Aparna Reddy: So we should say explicitly: for hosted API you don’t need a dedicated deployment. Just pick a model and call it.

[10:54] Henry Cho: That’s a copy change in email and maybe in the console empty state.

[10:58] Ben Carter: I can add a line: “No infra setup needed for Hosted API—just create a key and make your first call.”

[11:05] Aparna Reddy: Perfect.

[11:07] Dev Patel: Also mention rate limits. When they do load tests on day one, they hit a rate limit, then assume they’re blocked. If we can message: “If you’re load testing, consider Dedicated,” that’s both helpful and a sales-assist trigger.

[11:21] Ben Carter: Right, but we should not sound salesy.

[11:24] Aparna Reddy: Keep it developer-first. Something like “Need higher throughput? Here’s how to request a limit increase or evaluate Dedicated.”

[11:32] Marissa Cole: We can show a nudge only if we see repeated 429s.

[11:36] Paula Mendes: That’s doable. “After 3 rate_limit responses, show contextual help.”

[11:41] Henry Cho: That’s also a great experiment: do these nudges reduce drop-off after 429.

[11:47] Ben Carter: Okay, one more question: what’s the “most expensive” support scenario we should prevent?

[11:53] Dev Patel: The compliance / data retention one, honestly. People ask “do you train on my data” and “can I keep data in EU.” If we can link to the right docs, we reduce back-and-forth. But we must be precise.

[12:08] Aparna Reddy: Agree. And it’s not just compliance. Even startups ask it now.

[12:13] Ben Carter: We’ll keep it in an FAQ section at the bottom. “Security & privacy: here’s the doc.”

[12:20] Marissa Cole: Also, inside Console, the banner shouldn’t mention compliance unless they ask. But we can have a “Learn about data handling” link in settings.

[12:30] Paula Mendes: On instrumentation: can we track support_link_clicked from banners/emails? That’s a guardrail and a diagnostic.

[12:36] Dev Patel: Yes please. If that spikes, it means we made something worse.

[12:41] Henry Cho: Great. So action items: Aparna sends quotes, Dev drafts triage checklist, Marissa checks links/routes, Ben updates email modules, Paula and I align on properties.

[12:55] Aparna Reddy: Yep. And one last note: people trust proof points but they’re skeptical. They ask “how do you compare to Bedrock or OpenAI.” If we mention benchmarks, it has to be linked and not hand-wavy.

[13:08] Ben Carter: For sure. Soojin and Ethan are on that.

[13:12] Marissa Cole: Anything else? Maybe the “invite teammates” thing?

[13:16] Aparna Reddy: Less of an activation blocker, more of a retention lever. But yeah, teams that invite someone tend to stick. It’s just not a day-one problem.

[13:25] Henry Cho: Noted as a week-1/2 milestone.

[13:28] Ben Carter: Cool. I think that’s it. Thanks Aparna and Dev.

[13:32] Aparna Reddy: Yep. I’ll send the write-up after this.


Recap / Next steps (manual):
- Translate top 4 blocker buckets into email modules + console checklist steps
- Ensure all links used in emails route correctly in Console (avoid 404)
- Add troubleshooting content for 401/403/model_not_found/429 and include Support escalation
- Treat streaming as optional “next step” to avoid over-indexing on a higher-friction activation criterion
